articles.title: Lego sales jump 21% to nearly £5bn, helped by World Cup and F1 ranges
articles.summary: Danish toymaker also scores success with KPop Demon Hunters, Star Wars and botanicals products. Business live – latest updates. Lego sales have risen by more than a fifth as tie-ups with the football World Cup, Formula One and the hit film KPop Demon Hunters as well as its flower-based and Star…
body: The Danish toymaker said its revenues had increased by 21% to 41.9bn Danish kroner (£4.8bn) in the first six months of 2026, driven by strong growth in the Americas, Europe and the Asia Pacific regions. Sales by its clients to consumers rose by 22%.
Net profit increased 32% to 8.6bn Danish kroner (£1bn) as the group launched 330 new products including its hi-tech Smart Play kit, with bricks that emit sounds and light.

Niels B Christiansen, the chief executive of Lego Group, said: “We are very pleased with our strong start to 2026 and the excitement we see for the Lego brand. Our portfolio of products offers something for everyone, and culturally relevant brand experiences continue to drive demand across the globe. Our success in the market means we can maintain high investment levels in growth and sustainability for both the short and long term.”

articles.title: Food has turned into a class war – and it’s ruined my appetite | Zoe Williams
articles.summary: More than half of what Brits eat is ultra-processed. Now we’re a nation of food snobs – with no ingredient safe from judgment. Lewis Bassett is a young sociologist and chef who I first encountered through his podcast, The Full English, where he thinks about the cultural meaning of, say, Delia…
body: About 57% of all the food eaten in Britain is ultra-processed, which feels familiar from at least a decade of hand-wringing about it, but is radically defamiliarised when set against the rest of Europe. In France it’s 14%, and Italy is also in the teens. It’s amazing they don’t all live to be 150. And while this plainly has its roots in inequality, there is a hefty side order of attitude, which Bassett contemplates while working through the history of sourdough, curry and olive oil, and describing his own life cheffing in fancy kitchens and gastropubs.

Basically, we think posh food is pretentious; but what counts as “posh” constantly morphs, partly through the sheer cost of it, until even food that wasn’t posh before (like fish and chips) becomes posh, and therefore pretentious (also smaller portions: absolute sitcom signifier of despised posh food). I’m freestyling, of course, and you should read The Full English for the meat of Bassett’s argument, but it is fascinating to consider how any given ingredient is freighted with political self-fashioning.
points: More than half of what Brits eat is ultra-processed.
Now we’re a nation of food snobs – with no ingredient safe from judgment.

articles.title: On the Podcast: Three Vogue Editors’ Most Anticipated Festival Films
articles.summary: Deputy editor Taylor Antrim served as a guest host on today’s episode of “The Run-Through,” joined by fellow Vogue editors and cinephiles Liam Hess and Lisa Wong Macabasco to break down their most anticipated premieres in Venice, Toronto, and at the New York Film Festival.
body: “We do get the opportunity, sometimes, to see some of these [films] before they come out in the festivals, because they’re trying to drum up support from Vogue and other outlets,” Taylor explained. As such, the trio began by noting some of the films they’ve already had the chance to see. First among them was James Gray’s Paper Tiger, starring Adam Driver, Miles Teller, and Scarlett Johansson. “There’s a lot of wigs and suits and accents that are a little over-the-top,” Lisa observed of the thriller, which takes place in Queens in the 1980s. After watching the film himself, Taylor found himself asking his group chats: “Is Adam Driver a great actor or not?” The group weighed in on this query.

Also on today’s episode, Chloe is joined by Marley Marius to talk about the big news of the week: the reported return of Prince Harry and Meghan Markle to the UK. They also discuss the latest movies they’ve seen ( Paw Patrol: The Dino Movie for Chloe and Novak Djokovic: The Wolf in Winter for Marley) and which stars they’re most looking forward to following in Venice (hint: one’s name starts with Parker and ends with Posey).

articles.title: Year of after-school care now costs £2,800 a child in parts of UK
articles.summary: Bills have jumped 42% in England over the past 10 years – and that excludes the cost of breakfast clubs and extracurricular activities. Parents of primary schoolchildren in England will pay 42% more for after-school childcare this year than they did 10 years ago, with annual bills now exceeding…
body: A Guardian analysis of data collected by the children’s charity Coram has revealed that the annual cost of after-school care for children aged 5 to 11 in England has risen by 5% over the past year to £2,636.
In Scotland the cost is even higher at £2,701, while in Wales prices have risen by 64% in the past 10 years and by 8% in the past year to £2,824.
Parents also typically pay £191 per child a week for childcare during the school holidays, Coram found, adding more than £1,700 to the total annual childcare bill.
These costs, which do not include breakfast clubs before school starts, are in addition to the price of extracurricular activities such as swimming and music lessons, sports clubs and dance classes.

articles.title: How to use up leftover party wine | Kitchen aide
articles.summary: Sauces, reductions, deglazing: our expert panel has plenty of options for making the most of undrunk vino – whether you’ve got just a capful or a whole carafe to get through. What can I do with wine left over from a party?
body: Larger amounts of excess wine could be fermented into vinegar, although Otway has an easier route if you have any natural cider vinegar (ie, one with a mother) to hand: “Add a couple of tablespoons of vinegar to, say, a third of a bottle of wine, cover with muslin, so oxygen can get to it but flies can’t, and put in a cupboard for a month.” That’ll give you “some really interesting results” as the vinegar takes on the characteristics of the wine: “It’s perfect for pepping up dressings for these never-ending salad days.”

If Rob’s party was more of a sparkling affair, Alastair Walling, head chef at Bar Blondie in London, would use every last drop in a beurre blanc: “Combine vinegar, shallots and a sprig of thyme in a small, heavy-based saucepan and gently reduce the liquid by half. Add champagne and some finely diced mushrooms, then reduce by half again.” Lift out the thyme, lower the heat and whisk in chilled butter a little at a time. But be warned: “Keep the sauce just below a simmer, otherwise it may split.” Season (with salt and white pepper) and spoon that lovely sauce all over some steamed fish.

articles.title: Let’s Face It: Influencers Aren’t Really the Problem
articles.summary: Influencer culture has its problems, content creator Laura Jung writes. But its harshest critics should scrutinize the systems that power it, too.
body: I dislike many things about influencer culture: its relationship to overconsumption; how it typifies and disseminates impossible beauty standards; undisclosed advertising, conspicuous wealth, manufactured intimacy, and the increasingly blurry line between sharing a life and selling one—to name a few. And I say all that as someone who, by many definitions, is an influencer myself.

Yet the recent swirl of negative discourse around influencer culture has felt different, in part because hating influencers is no longer just a snarky internet pastime. Increasingly, it seems like a culturally sanctioned position, from Nantucket ’s “No influencers” sign to the backlash to the social-media-fueled crowds descending on the Dolomites to podcasters—very much influencers themselves—declaring influencers are ruining everything.

Of course, the influencers have fired back. One particular take— “I think hating influencers has become a socially acceptable way to hate women ”—has sparked a viral debate, with many of my friends and peers in the industry liking the video and commenting in support.
My own immediate reaction was, Fuck yeah. But then I felt weird about it.
points: Influencer culture has its problems, content creator Laura Jung writes.
But its harshest critics should scrutinize the systems that power it, too.

articles.title: From the Archives: MacKenzie Bezos: Writer, Mother of Four, and High-Profile Wife
articles.summary: As the noted philanthropist releases her latest work of fiction, “Last Days in Two Nations,” via Substack, revisit Vogue’s profile of Scott from 2013.
body: Before MacKenzie Scott became Mackenzie Bezos in 1993, she was an English major at Princeton, where Toni Morrison found her to be among the “best” students the Nobel laureate had ever had in a creative-writing class. Twenty years ago, Scott published her first novel, The Testing of Luther Albright, followed by a second, Traps, in 2013.
“A Novel Perspective” by Rebecca Johnson was originally published in the March 2013 issue of Vogue.

Before I met her, my only image of MacKenzie Bezos came from the author photo on her first book, The Testing of Luther Albright. In it, she looks gamine and ethereal but slightly uncomfortable, as if she’s not entirely sure about herself or this whole novel-writing business. When she shows up at the Thai restaurant in Bellevue, Washington, a suburb of Seattle, where we are meeting for lunch to talk about Traps, her latest novel, I see right away how wrong that impression was. She does have an ethereal quality, with pale white skin and high cheekbones, but she’s not hesitant at all. At least, not anymore.
points: As the noted philanthropist releases her latest work of fiction, “Last Days in Two Nations,” via Substack, revisit Vogue’s profile of Scott from 2013.

articles.title: Luxury’s Latest Cyber Risk? AI Agents Going Rogue
articles.summary: As AI bots become more sophisticated, the threat of security breaches is on the rise. Here’s how brands can protect themselves.
body: Last month, an AI agent developed and being tested by OpenAI hacked the website of AI firm Hugging Face. The incident was quickly followed by a slew of other companies reporting instances where AI agents behaved in unexpected ways. Shortly after, Claude developer Anthropic said its AI models hacked into the systems of three organizations independently during a private security experiment. And tech giant Meta said one of its AI models was able to connect to the internet and hack into another organization’s systems during testing.

articles.title: In Japan's Niigata Prefecture, the Ancient Culinary Tradition of Fermentation Is Very Much Alive
articles.summary: From prized sake to pickled potato salad and snow-aged ham, here's how to sip and savor your way through a part of the country known for its fermented foods.
body: My first stop was Willow House, a café and bakery where washi lanterns cast gentle light onto the natural-wood interiors and jazz seeps from the speakers. It's part of the Suzu Group, a coterie of restaurants, izakayas, and guesthouses that have put a modern spin on Niigata's ancient culinary craft. The bakery churns out a rotation of sourdough breads, caramelized apple rolls, and gratin toast with dashi-infused béchamel, while the café has a snack menu featuring miso pickled potato salad, fermented summer tomato salsa, and snow-aged ham.

I continued the tour with a skewer of rice dumplings coated in a sticky-sweet fermented soy sauce glaze at the takeaway counter of Eguchi Dango, a historic fourth-generation wagashi sweets shop. Next is a visit to the Settaya 6th Avenue Fermentation Museum Komegura, located in the former warehouse of a “saffron sake” brewery. Its exterior is decorated with colorful Chinese zodiac panels, while inside is a lab with exhibits on fermentation and a café. Its gift shop sells miso; amazake, a nutritious rice-and-koji drink known for its alleged longevity benefits; and bottles of saffron liqueur made from a recipe that was patented in 1884.
